notes.heading: Interpret elimination as a statement about all shared solutions
paragraphs: Elimination combines equations that every shared solution must satisfy. When the variables disappear, the remaining statement distinguishes coincident equations from inconsistent ones. Parameters require case splits where coefficients become zero. A nonlinear equation can intersect a line twice, once or not at all, so substituting an expression should be followed by solving and checking all candidates. A numerical answer is only part of a modelling task: restrictions such as nonnegative integer counts can make an algebraically consistent solution infeasible.

questions.prompt: Solve x+y=4 and x+ky=6 for real x,y, distinguishing k=1 from other real k.
questions.answer: For k≠1, y=2/(k-1) and x=4-2/(k-1). For k=1 there is no solution.
solution: Subtract the first equation to obtain (k-1)y=2.
Divide only for k≠1; when k=1 the statement 0=2 is impossible.
markingPoints: Give both values in the nonzero case.

questions.prompt: Solve x+y=5 and x²+y²=13 over the reals, giving all ordered pairs.
solution: Factor to obtain x=2 or 3, then recover y and check both equations.
markingPoints: Give and check both ordered pairs.

questions.prompt: A fictional venue sells only 4-unit and 7-unit tickets. Exactly 10 tickets bring in 53 units. Show whether nonnegative whole-number counts can satisfy the data.
questions.answer: No. If n counts 7-unit tickets, 7n+4(10-n)=53 gives n=13/3, which is not an integer.
solution: Use both the ticket-count and revenue constraints.
Distinguish a real algebraic solution from a permissible count.
markingPoints: Reject it for whole-number ticket counts.
